title: Biometric Skin Patch Surveillance: The Body as Data Terminal
body:
Biometric skin patches, commercially designated as DermLog units in most GLMZ corporate zones, are thin-film biosensors adhered directly to the epidermis that continuously harvest physiological telemetry from the wearer. Manufactured primarily by Somatech Dynamics and licensed to corporate HR divisions under bulk indenture agreements, the patches monitor heart rate variability, galvanic skin response, cortisol fluctuation, blood oxygen saturation, and micro-tremor patterns at the wrist or neck. Data streams are transmitted via low-power body-area network protocols to collection nodes embedded in building infrastructure, where they are aggregated into real-time physiological profiles. The patches are self-adhesive, water-resistant, and designed for continuous 30-day wear cycles, with replacements issued at corporate health kiosks as a standard employment benefit at Tier 3 and below.

The ostensible purpose of DermLog units is occupational health monitoring. Employers cite heat stress prevention in logistics facilities, fatigue detection in piloting and heavy machinery contexts, and early-warning metabolic screening as justifications for mandatory deployment. In practice, the physiological data is cross-referenced against behavioral analytics platforms to generate what Somatech calls Emotional Reliability Scores — composite indices that flag workers exhibiting sustained stress responses, anomalous cortisol spikes correlated with interrogation-adjacent scenarios, or heart rate patterns consistent with deception-adjacent cognitive load. These scores feed directly into performance review systems without worker notification in most sub-Tier 4 employment contracts, which include mandatory biosensor consent clauses buried in onboarding documentation.

The social implications of continuous physiological surveillance are severe and layered. Workers in monitored environments report chronic behavioral modification, a condition colloquially termed 'patch paranoia,' in which individuals consciously attempt to regulate their own stress responses to avoid triggering algorithmic flags. This produces a feedback loop of anxiety that itself elevates the cortisol readings the worker is attempting to suppress. Medical researchers in the Academic Enclave districts have documented a statistically significant increase in autonomic nervous system dysregulation among long-term patch wearers, a condition the manufacturers dispute by citing study methodology. Black market vendors in the Undercroft districts sell electromagnetic shielding adhesives marketed as 'patch blockers,' though possession of such devices constitutes contract violation in most indenture agreements and is treated as grounds for immediate termination.

Tier availability follows a predictable inversion: the higher the corporate tier, the less invasive the monitoring. Tier 5 and above executives wear voluntary wellness patches that collect data stored in personal health vaults with explicit access controls. Tier 3 and below workers wear mandatory compliance patches whose data streams are owned by the employer under Neural and Biological Data Acquisition clauses standardized after the 2181 Meridian Corporate Compact. Unaffiliated citizens in gray zones and refugee settlements have no access to the legitimate health data the patches generate, though counterfeit versions running open-source firmware circulate widely and are used for personal health tracking without the employer data uplink.
